title: Area V review: Air Traffic Control Clearances and Procedures
intro: These questions mix the two Tasks of Area V: copying, reading back, interpreting and flying an ATC clearance, and complying with departure, en route and arrival procedures. Most put a clearance inside a procedure the way your learner will meet it: a hold for release before a VFR departure, a climb via SID with a changed top altitude, a runway change on an RNAV SID, a cruise clearance, a charted hold, a descend via STAR that is amended or interrupted, and a radio failure while being vectored.

questions.q: Your learner phones for his clearance at a nontowered field under a 3,000-foot broken layer with 10 miles visibility. He gets "hold for release, expect a 30-minute departure delay." He wants to leave VFR now and pick up his IFR clearance from Center once airborne, probably at 2,500 feet in hills where the MEA is 4,000. What do you teach before he goes?
options: He must wait on the ground: "hold for release" holds the airplane until ATC issues a release time, whether he plans to leave under VFR or IFR
He may leave VFR with the IFR flight plan still open and his assigned code set, then call Center for the release in the air
He may leave VFR after canceling IFR and setting a VFR code, but a later clearance is not promised, and below the MEA the terrain is his
He may leave VFR after canceling IFR, and once Center clears him at 2,500 feet, the controller takes over his terrain and obstacle clearance
questions.why: "Hold for release" applies to the IFR clearance and does not prevent a VFR departure, but before takeoff the pilot should cancel the IFR flight plan and use the appropriate VFR code, and an IFR clearance may not be available after departure [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]. A pilot who departs VFR and accepts a clearance below the MEA, MIA, MVA or OROCA is responsible for his own terrain and obstruction clearance until reaching it, and should tell the controller if he cannot keep it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-9]]. So Center does not take over the terrain at 2,500, and leaving with the IFR plan open and the IFR code set is what the AIM says not to do.

questions.q: At a towered field your learner copies: "Cessna 5432K cleared to Johnston airport, Scott One departure, Jonez transition, then as filed. Climb via SID except maintain 5,000. Departure 125.35, squawk 4321." The SID shows two "at or above" crossing altitudes below 5,000 and a top altitude of 7,000. What readback and what climb do you teach?
options: Read back the clearance with "except maintain 5,000" and the call sign; fly the SID path and its published restrictions, and stop at 5,000
Read back each charted crossing altitude so the controller can check them all, and then climb via the SID up to its 7,000-foot top altitude
Read back the clearance with 5,000 and the call sign; the "except" cancels the charted restrictions, so climb straight up to 5,000
Read back only the code and the frequency, since the SID itself already holds the altitudes, then climb via the SID to the 7,000 top altitude
questions.why: The IFH recommends reading the IFR clearance back to clearance delivery [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. Read back altitudes, altitude restrictions and vectors in the order given, include the call sign, and do not read back altitudes from charted procedures unless the controller states them [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]. "Climb via SID except maintain (altitude)" requires the SID lateral path and its published speed and altitude restrictions while climbing, and the climb stops at the assigned altitude until ATC clears more [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]]. The "except" changes only the top altitude, which becomes the assigned 5,000 [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9h6]]; it does not cancel the crossing restrictions, and the charted 7,000 no longer applies.

questions.q: Your learner's clearance routes him on an airway and to hold at the Brookwood VOR, which a NOTAM shows out of service. His airplane has an IFR-approved panel GPS with a current database. He asks whether he has to refuse the route. What do you teach?
options: Refuse it: an airway and a hold that are based on a VOR can be flown only with that VOR's own signal, so he must ask for another route
Accept it and tune the VOR anyway: if he can hear its identifier, the NOTAM is out of date and the signal may be used in the normal way
Accept it only if ATC promises radar vectors along the route, since only vectors can replace a VOR that is out of service on an airway
Accept it and use the panel GPS as a substitute for the VOR on the route and in the hold, advising ATC of that plan if it is needed
questions.why: A suitable RNAV system, such as an IFR-approved GPS, may be used as a substitute means of navigation when a VOR is out of service, including holding over it, and the database should be current [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]. Pilots planning this may need to advise ATC of their intent and capability [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]; a pilot without such equipment must notify ATC immediately that he cannot receive the signals the clearance needs [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]. Do not fly a procedure NOTAMed out of service even if the identification is present [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]], so hearing the identifier proves nothing, and nothing in these sources makes radar vectors the only substitute.

questions.q: Your learner plans an IFR flight in his Cessna 172 from a satellite airport near Kennedy to Atlantic City by tower en route control. From the route list in the figure he picks DIXIE V1 HOWIE at 8,000. What do you correct?
options: Nothing: any route listed to the destination may be filed, and he should write "TEC" in the route box in place of the listed airways
File the props route, DIXIE V229 ACY, at or below its 6,000-foot highest altitude, and write "TEC" in the flight plan remarks
He can't use TEC from a satellite airport: the program serves only the major airports printed in the list's left-hand column
File the props route but at 8,000, because the altitude column of the list is a minimum altitude, much like an airway MEA
questions.why: When more than one route is listed to the same destination, the pilot must make sure the route for his aircraft classification is filed, and the altitude column shows the highest altitude allowed for the route [[29:70|IPH 2-10]] [[29:71|IPH 2-11]]. In the figure DIXIE V1 HOWIE is for jets only, and the props route to Atlantic City shows 6,000. The first column is the approach control area in which the departure airport lies [[29:70|IPH 2-10]], so a satellite field there qualifies, and flights may also be planned to satellite airports near the primary destination via the same routing [[29:71|IPH 2-11]]. Pilots request TEC by putting "TEC" in the remarks section [[33:221|AIM 4-1-19]]. Routes are effective only during each terminal facility's normal hours, so check NOTAMs that they will be operating [[29:71|IPH 2-11]].

questions.q: Center clears your learner "cruise 6,000" to a nontowered destination that has an RNAV (GPS) approach; the MEA on his airway is 5,000. He asks two things: may he drop to 5,000 for a smoother ride and later go back to 6,000, and does he still need an approach clearance? What do you answer?
options: He may move anywhere in the block, back up to 6,000 included, and the cruise clearance already approves the approach
He may descend to 5,000 when he likes but not climb back after reporting leaving 6,000, and cruise approves the approach
He may descend only after asking Center, since the block is just for planning, and he needs a separate approach clearance
He may descend to 5,000 and later climb back to 6,000, but he must still get a separate approach clearance from Center
questions.why: "Cruise" assigns a block from the minimum IFR altitude up to and including the cruise altitude; climb and descent within it are at the pilot's discretion, but once he starts down and reports leaving an altitude in the block he may not return to it without another clearance [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]. The P/CG adds that a cruise clearance is also approval to proceed to and make an approach at the destination airport [[34:332|P/CG C-11]], and that an instrument letdown there must follow a standard or special IAP for that airport [[34:333|P/CG C-12]]. The tempting "separate approach clearance" answer misses that approval.

questions.q: Center tells your learner, "Cessna 5432K, hold southeast of PINNE as published, expect further clearance 1645," as in the left half of the figure. He complains that he got no leg length or turn direction and plans to cross PINNE at cruise speed and sort it out there. What do you teach?
options: Hold in a standard right-turn pattern on the course he used to reach PINNE, since ATC gave him no turns or leg length
Refuse the hold until Center reads complete instructions; a clearance with no leg length cannot be flown as it was given
Hold as charted at PINNE, ask for full instructions only if he wants them, and start slowing 3 minutes before the fix
Hold as charted at PINNE but cross it at cruise speed, then slow to holding speed during the entry to save some time
questions.why: When the pattern is charted, ATC may omit all holding instructions except the charted direction and the words AS PUBLISHED, and the pilot is expected to hold as depicted; ATC must give complete instructions when the pilot asks for them [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]] [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]. When 3 minutes or less from a clearance limit with no clearance beyond it, the pilot starts a speed reduction so as to cross the fix at or below the maximum holding airspeed [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]]. A standard pattern on the inbound course is the fallback only when no pattern is charted and no instructions could be obtained [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8]].

questions.q: In ground school you show your learner this MVA chart. He recalls that approach once vectored him at 2,000 in the sector labeled 2000, although the airway he had just left had an MEA of 3,000. He asks whether that was legal and what he should have done. What do you answer?
options: Legal: terminal controllers may vector IFR aircraft at MVAs below published altitudes, and he should query any that seems too low
Not legal: ATC may never give an IFR aircraft an altitude below the MEA of the airway it has just left, so he should have refused it
Legal, because MVAs are printed on the en route charts for pilots, so he could have checked the 2,000 himself before descending
Legal only in VMC: in IMC a controller must keep an IFR aircraft at or above the airway's MEA until it is cleared for the approach
questions.why: Terminal controllers can assign altitudes lower than published procedural altitudes, called minimum vectoring altitudes; these are displayed at the controller's position and are not published or accessible to pilots, and a pilot assigned an altitude that seems too low should query the controller before descending [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]. The controller vectors IFR aircraft at or above the MVA, and the pilot promptly complies but questions any altitude he believes is incorrect [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]. So the 2,000 was proper, the en route chart is not where he would find it, and the rule is the MVA, not the MEA of the airway behind him.

questions.q: Your learner, flying his turboprop single, is cleared to "descend via the KOLTS Two arrival, runway 28 transition, except after RAMMS maintain 11,000." Leaving 16,000, he is handed off to approach. Which check-in follows the AIM?
options: "N23X, leaving 16,000, descending via the KOLTS Two arrival, runway 28 transition"
"N23X, level 16,000 on the KOLTS Two arrival, runway 28 transition, request descent"
"N23X, descending via the KOLTS Two arrival, runway 28 transition, restrictions as published"
"N23X, leaving 16,000 for 11,000, descending via the KOLTS Two arrival, runway 28 transition"
questions.why: Under "descend via," on initial contact with each new frequency the pilot reports the altitude leaving, "descending via" and the procedure name, the runway transition or landing direction if assigned, and any assigned restrictions not published on the procedure; the AIM's example with a changed bottom altitude says "leaving flight level one niner zero for one two thousand" [[33:395|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. An "except after (fix) maintain (altitude)" clearance is such an unpublished restriction [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]], so leaving out the 11,000 is the tempting error. He is already cleared to descend at pilot's discretion to meet the published restrictions [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]], so requesting descent is wrong, and a check-in without the altitude leaving gives the controller nothing to check.

questions.q: Your learner has an RNAV SID for runway 28L loaded in his G1000. Taxiing out, ground changes him to runway 1R with the same SID and transition, and he reads back the runway. At the hold line the tower says, "RNAV to KAYAK, runway 1R, cleared for takeoff." The flight plan still shows the 28L legs. What do you teach?
options: Tell the tower he needs a moment, then load and check the SID for 1R, and report at once if a different SID ends up loaded
Take off and fix the flight plan in the climb, since the KAYAK advisory shows ATC expects the change to take some time
Take off and go direct KAYAK, because the advisory means ATC has replaced the runway legs of the SID with a direct
Take off, since his runway readback already told ATC about the change, and ATC will vector him if the old legs mislead him
questions.why: Pilots assigned an RNAV DP who receive a change of runway, transition or procedure must verify that the changes are loaded and available for navigation [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]]. ATC may name the initial waypoint to remind pilots to verify the correct procedure is programmed before takeoff, pilots must immediately advise ATC if a different RNAV SID is entered, and the SID is still flown as published, so the advisory is not a direct clearance [[33:348|AIM 5-2-8]]. The runway readback is part of the departure clearance readback [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]], but it does not program the box. Accepting or refusing a clearance is the pilot's responsibility [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]], and a pilot who needs to delay an operation is expected to tell ATC [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

questions.q: Tower clears your learner: "Cessna 5432K, runway 11, fly runway heading, climb and maintain 3,000, cleared for takeoff." The airport diagram shows runway 11's centerline at 112 degrees magnetic, and a strong north wind is blowing. He briefs a 10-degree crab into the wind to track the extended centerline. What do you teach?
options: Fly 110 degrees, the number painted on the runway, with no wind correction, because runway heading means the runway number
Crab as briefed: ATC expects his ground track to follow the extended centerline, so any heading that holds it is correct
Fly 112 degrees with no wind correction until ATC says otherwise, and read back runway 11 with the rest of the clearance
Fly 112 degrees until reaching 3,000, then crab into the wind, since wind correction is withheld only in the initial climb
questions.why: Pilots cleared to fly or maintain runway heading are expected to fly the published magnetic heading of the extended runway centerline, from the airport diagram and not the painted numbers, and not to apply drift correction, which prevents a loss of separation between parallel departures [[29:58|IPH 1-42]]. An assigned heading is flown promptly and held until further instructions [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]], so reaching 3,000 does not start a crab. The initial readback of a departure clearance includes the runway assignment [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

questions.q: Your learner's home field is nontowered. Its takeoff minimums read "Rwy 32, standard with minimum climb of 410' per NM to 3000' or 1100-3 for VCOA." On a hot afternoon his POH data shows only about 350 feet per NM, the weather is above the VCOA minimums, and his clearance includes the ODP. What do you teach?
options: Go as cleared: a climb gradient printed with an ODP is planning advice and is not binding on a pilot flying under Part 91
Go as cleared: once departure says "radar contact," ATC takes over obstacle clearance for the rest of the climb
Go as cleared, and if the climb falls short of 410 feet per NM, switch to the VCOA and tell ATC once he is level
Fly the VCOA, which today's weather allows, and tell ATC before takeoff; without that option he would wait for VMC
questions.why: A climb gradient on a DP that is part of the ATC clearance is mandatory unless increased takeoff minimums are provided and the weather allows them [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e5]]. The VCOA is developed as an alternative to a climb gradient over 200 feet per NM: it is flown in visual conditions at or above its ceiling and visibility, and pilots must advise ATC of their intent to fly it before departure [[33:353|AIM 5-2-9e7]] [[29:58|IPH 1-42]], so switching to it once airborne is wrong. The IPH adds that a pilot who cannot maintain the ODP climb gradient must wait until he can depart under VMC [[29:59|IPH 1-43]], and "radar contact" does not relieve the pilot of terrain and obstruction clearance [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]].

questions.q: Eastbound at 6,000 on a Victor airway, your learner sees that the MEA rises to 9,000 past the next VOR, with an eastbound MCA of 8,000 at the VOR. Center says, "Cessna 5432K, climb at pilot's discretion, maintain 9,000." He plans to stay at 6,000 in smooth air until over the VOR. What do you teach?
options: Fine as planned: with a pilot's discretion clearance ATC takes on the terrain until he reaches 9,000
Climb before the VOR: discretion sets when he starts, but he must still cross the VOR at or above 8,000
Fine as planned, provided he starts climbing right after passing the VOR, as 14 CFR 91.177(b) says
Climb now at the best rate: an MCA ahead cancels pilot's discretion and makes an immediate climb due
questions.why: "At pilot's discretion" lets the pilot start the climb when he wishes and climb at any rate [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]], but a clearance is never authorization to deviate from any rule, regulation or minimum altitude [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]]. Climb to a higher minimum IFR altitude begins right after passing the point where it applies, except that when ground obstructions intervene that point must be crossed at or above the MCA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(b)]]. MCAs are established where obstacles prevent a normal climb to the higher MEA after the fix [[2:69|Chart Users' Guide p 69]], so "climb right after the VOR" is the tempting error. The clearance does not give ATC the terrain, and the MCA does not cancel the discretion; he plans his climb to meet it.

questions.q: In the training device you play Center: "Cessna 5432K, turn left heading 270, vectors to Kewanee VOR, maintain 5,000." A minute later you fail his radios. He is in IMC, no expected altitude was ever given, and the MEA on his cleared airway beyond Kewanee is 6,000. Which plan meets 14 CFR 91.185?
options: Fly direct to Kewanee from where the radios failed, then his cleared route beyond it at 6,000, the higher of 5,000 and the MEA
Hold heading 270 at 5,000 until Kewanee is abeam, since the vector was his last clearance, then turn onto the route at 5,000
Turn direct to the destination and climb to the altitude he filed, since without vectors the filed route and altitude apply
Keep heading 270 at 5,000 and wait for ATC to call, since a pilot being vectored may never leave a heading on his own
questions.why: In IMC, a pilot being radar vectored when the radios fail flies the direct route from the point of radio failure to the fix, route or airway specified in the vector clearance [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(ii)]], at the highest of the last assigned altitude, the minimum IFR altitude and any expected altitude for the route segment being flown [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]. Beyond Kewanee that is the 6,000 MEA, not the 5,000 he was given. The filed route comes last, only when there is no assigned or expected route [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(iv)]], and holding the old heading is not the direct route the rule names.

questions.q: Descending via an RNAV STAR, your learner hears, "Cessna 5432K, turn left heading 250, vectors for sequencing, maintain 8,000." He starts deleting the STAR waypoints to build a direct leg to the approach and keeps planning for the STAR's next speed restriction. What do you teach?
options: Keep the STAR's altitude and speed restrictions on the heading, since a vector for sequencing changes only his lateral path
Fly 250 at 8,000; the STAR and its published restrictions are canceled, but keep its waypoints in case ATC clears him back
Fly 250 at 8,000 and keep the STAR's published speeds, because speed restrictions stand apart from altitude restrictions
Fly 250 at 8,000 and delete the STAR legs now, because an aircraft vectored off a STAR is never cleared back onto it
questions.why: If vectored or cleared off a STAR, pilots must consider it canceled, along with its published altitude and speed restrictions; ATC gives an altitude and, if necessary, a speed, and says where to expect to resume if it intends to clear the aircraft back onto the STAR [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]] [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]. RNAV STARs may be amended by vectors or direct clearances, and pilots should avoid premature deletion of waypoints so they can rejoin [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]]. Published speed restrictions are independent of altitude restrictions [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]], which makes keeping them tempting, but a vector off the STAR cancels its speed restrictions too [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

questions.q: Your learner is flying his turboprop single on a STAR under a "descend via" clearance. Approach says, "N23X, descend and maintain 6,000," with no new route and nothing about the STAR's crossing altitudes. The next fix has a published speed restriction. What does the AIM say still applies?
options: Nothing on the STAR applies now: a new altitude cancels its lateral path, crossing altitudes and published speeds together
All of it applies: the crossing altitudes bind until ATC cancels each one by name, and the published speeds apply as well
Only the crossing altitudes still apply, since a speed restriction always ends when the altitude to maintain is changed
The lateral path and published speeds apply, but the omitted crossing altitudes are canceled, and he descends to 6,000
questions.why: When the altitude to maintain is changed or restated and earlier altitude restrictions are omitted, those restrictions are canceled, including STAR altitude restrictions [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10g]]. Published speed restrictions are independent of altitude restrictions and are mandatory unless ATC modifies them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a1]], and the AIM's "cleared (STAR) arrival, descend and maintain (altitude)" example keeps the lateral path and requires the published speeds [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1a2]]. Only a vector or a clearance off the STAR cancels the procedure itself [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1a2]].

questions.q: Descending via an RNAV STAR in IMC, your learner's G1000 announces a loss of GPS integrity, and the magenta line can no longer be trusted. He wants to keep flying the STAR by heading and time and mention the problem at the next handoff. What do you teach?
options: Squawk 7600 and fly the STAR's lost communications track, since a failed navigator falls under the radio failure rule
Keep flying the STAR by heading and time to the next fix and report the failure there, to keep the frequency clear
Tell ATC at once, "failure of GPS, unable RNAV, request amended clearance," and navigate on another source
Finish the STAR on a tablet's GPS app, which is accurate enough for terminal use, and then ask for vectors
questions.why: If unable to comply with the requirements of an RNAV or RNP procedure, pilots must advise ATC as soon as possible, for example, "failure of GPS system, unable RNAV, request amended clearance" [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]]. Pilots encountering navigation error events should transition to another source of navigation and request amended clearances as necessary [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]], and must report in-flight malfunctions of navigation equipment to ATC as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]], not at a later handoff. 14 CFR 91.185 covers two-way radio communications failure, not a failed navigator [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(a)]], and a hand-held GPS is only an aid to situational awareness under IFR [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]].
